title: api(resources): RULING — reduce :scope policy to two shapes (:rf.scope/global | {:from-db id}) and make clear-scope take a concrete scope
description:
_Filed 2026-09-05 12:37:46 AUSEST by the API-review wave-3 coordinator from resources.md (ref resources.3); parent epic rf2-kuky. Local-only dossiers: ai/findings/API-review/{fable,codex}/ (gitignored; may be deleted)._

## Problem

`reg-resource`'s `:scope` policy gate admits FIVE shapes (`implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/registry.cljc:75–112` `valid-scope-policy?`; resolution arms `:796–870` `resolve-scope-for-event`), a route entry admits a sixth (`route.cljc:507–560`, the anonymous `(fn [route ctx] …)` tier), and `:rf.resource/clear-scope` admits two payload forms (`events.cljc:2144–2214`). The corpus uses two policy shapes across all 13 `reg-resource` registrations in 4 apps + 1 testbed (`:rf.scope/global` ×5, `{:from-db <id>}` ×8) and one clear-scope form (a concrete scope pre-resolved with `resolve-resource-scope`). The other shapes exist only in tests, spec and docs, and two of them carry dedicated diagnostic subsystems that exist for no other reason.

| Shape | Lowers to | app / tool / testbed | tests |
|---|---|---|---|
| B3 `:scope :rf.scope/from-caller` | "every ensure/refetch/sub MUST pass `:scope`" + `:rf.error/resource-scope-required-from-caller` (`registry.cljc:846–855`) + the dev heuristic `:rf.warning/resource-sub-scope-mismatch` (`subs.cljc:121–272`, ~150 lines; the ONLY policy it fires for, `:229–240`) | 0 | 35 lines / 16 files |
| B4 `:scope (fn [] …)` fn-of-nothing | `(policy)` at `registry.cljc:864–866` (arm 3d) | 0 | 1 (`resources_skeleton_cljs_test.cljs:277`) |
| B5 `:scope <literal EDN>` at registration | `canonicalize-scope` of a constant (`:867–868`, arm 3e) | 0 | 0 |
| B6 route entry `:scope (fn [route ctx] …)` | anonymous per-entry resolver (`route.cljc:544–546`); 016 `:239` already reserves `[:runtime path]` inputs as its NAMED replacement | 0 | 7 (`resources_route_cljs_test.cljc:591,675,2086`; `resource_algebra_view_cljs_test.cljc:163`; `routing/test/…/route_algebra_view_test.clj:178,210`; `tools/xray/test/…/resources_helpers_cljs_test.cljc:85`) |
| D2 `[:rf.resource/clear-scope {:scope {:from-db id}}]` | resolved against clear-scope's OWN coeffect db (`events.cljc:2185–2213`); from a logout handler's `:fx` that is the POST-logout db → nil → `:rf.warning/resource-clear-scope-unresolved` + no-op | 0 | 2 deftests (`resources_from_db_scope_cljs_test.cljc:290–333`), both dispatching clear-scope directly against a db that STILL holds the user — an ordering a logout handler cannot produce |
| E `:rf.resource/adopt-owner` / `:rf.resource/release-owner-identities` | planner-only primitives rowed beside app events in 016 §Events (`:624,:631`) yet "a framework primitive … never an app verb" (`:1347`); dispatched only by `route.cljc` | 0 | 14 (`resources_route_cljs_test` ×9, `resources_route_replan_cljs_test` ×5) |

D1, the form every doc, skill and test of the logout idiom uses (`auth.cljs:252–262`; `docs/resources/concepts.md:208`; `docs/core/how-to/add-auth.md:383`; `skills/re-frame2/patterns/resources.md:128`; `spec/016:149–163`), pre-resolves with `(rf/resolve-resource-scope db :realworld/session)` — a pure fn over a value that is honest about time. Spec 016 needs a dedicated subsection (`:149–163`), a warning op (`009:2054`) and that helper to steer authors OFF D2.

## Options

**O1 — fable (full reduction).** `:scope` is data with two shapes: `:rf.scope/global` (the explicit claim) | `{:from-db <id>}` (a name). Route entries, sub queries and event payloads INHERIT the registration policy; a use-site `:scope` is an OVERRIDE (a concrete scope or a `{:from-db …}`), retained for the admin-reads-tenant-X case, never required. Delete B3 with its error id and the whole `resource-sub-scope-mismatch` heuristic; delete B4, B5, B6; `clear-scope` takes a concrete scope only (delete the `{:from-db …}` arm and `:rf.warning/resource-clear-scope-unresolved`); move E to `:rf.resource.internal/*` beside `succeeded` / `failed` / `stale-fired` / `gc-fired` (11 internal ids already exist). Fable's answer to the counter: every principal in a re-frame2 app already lives in app-db — that is what app-db is for — so "known only at the caller" is "not yet named"; the fail-closed nil of a named resolver refuses to guess exactly as `from-caller` did, without a second mechanism; and a genuinely per-call resource passes a concrete `:scope` override on each ensure and sub — the same obligation `from-caller` imposed, minus the policy keyword.

**O2 — codex (keep the policies; teach).** "The proposed two-policy restriction is not yet justified. A literal tenant/sandbox scope is ordinary useful data, not a redundant resolver language. `:rf.scope/from-caller` says 'there is no default'; replacing it with global-plus-overrides loses that fail-closed requirement. A named resolver reading an otherwise unnecessary db slot also adds friction and state. 'Every principal lives in app-db' is not a demonstrated universal constraint: a multi-tenant inspector or reusable per-call resource can legitimately receive its subject as an argument. Retain concrete and caller-required policies. The anonymous function cases are more plausible pruning candidates, but deserve a separate decision about route-context information that db-only resolvers cannot currently express." On D2: "clear-scope's reference form means resolve against the clearing event's world; a concrete scope means act on a previously selected identity. Logout needs the latter … That timing difference is a teaching obligation, not proof that the former has no valid use. Preserve both unless intentionally narrowing the contract." On E: "demote planner-owned events without inventing a new public lifecycle" (concurs).

**O3 — Grok's middle (sequence, then rule).** D and E now (mechanical; D2's only claimed use has zero consumers and its tests exercise an ordering the headline case cannot produce — "the helper exists because of that time-travel bug; keeping the descriptor form so programmers can select a tenant does not fix the logout case, which is the only app consumer"). B4/B5/B6 with D (zero consumers, anonymous places → named things; the route-entry `:scope` SLOT stays as a data override, so codex's explicit tenant selection is preserved as data rather than as a fn). B3 last, after `@resources.1` / `@resources.2` land: "decide whether `:rf.scope/from-caller` is still a policy or just a way of saying 'override required'. I would delete it — every principal already lives in app-db."

## Recommendation

O1, sequenced as O3: rule all of (a)–(e) but file (d)+(e) and (b)+(c) as the first implementation beads and (a) as the last, so the `from-caller` deletion lands on a tree where the default-plus-override teaching (from `@resources.2`) is already written. The corpus argument is strong on every row: zero consumers after 13 registrations, 8 route plans and every sub in five apps had the opportunity; B3 is the anti-name ("someone else will say") and the sole reason a ~150-line heuristic and a use-time error exist; B6 is a place where 016 already reserves a name; D2 asks the NEXT event to look at a world that no longer exists. Codex's counter is carried honestly: if Mike wants a spelling for "there is no default", the fallback is to keep ONLY `:rf.scope/from-caller` (with its error and the heuristic that exists for it) and still delete (b)–(e). A per-call resource under O1 is modelled as a resolver reading a db slot the caller sets first, or as a concrete `:scope` override on every ensure and sub.

## Simpler elegant target

```clojure
;; A. revalidation is a FRAME property, like URL ownership. No fns.
(rf/make-frame {:id :app :url-bound? true :revalidate-on #{:focus :reconnect}})
[rf/frame-root {:id app-frame :url-bound? true :revalidate-on #{:focus :reconnect}} [root-view]]
;; absent key / re-registration without it → listeners removed (the `:url-bound? false` relinquish rule)

;; B. scope policy is DATA with two shapes — a claim or a name
(rf/reg-resource :realworld/feed {:scope {:from-db :realworld/session} …} request-fn)
(rf/reg-resource :realworld/tags {:scope :rf.scope/global …} request-fn)
;; route entries and sub queries INHERIT the registration policy; `:scope` there is an OVERRIDE
;; (a concrete scope or a `{:from-db …}`), retained for the admin-reads-tenant-X case, never required.

;; C. one registrar arity; the whole-db case spells its own lowering
(rf/reg-resource-scope :realworld/session
  {:inputs {:username [:db [:auth :user :username]]}}
  (fn [{:keys [username]} _] (when username [:rf.scope/session {:username username}])))
(rf/reg-resource-scope :app/everything {:inputs {:db [:db []]}} (fn [{:keys [db]} _] …))   ;; was the sugar

;; D. clear-scope takes a CONCRETE scope; resolve-resource-scope is how you get one
[:rf.resource/clear-scope {:scope (rf/resolve-resource-scope db :realworld/session) :cause :logout}]
```

## Why this is better (ethos)

-  **Data before magic / Low hidden context** (`spec/Principles.md:46,87`). A frame's revalidation policy is a fact about the frame; today it is a

  side effect the app must sequence after a commit-owned two-pass render, and the corpus proves the cost — the only consumer needed a paragraph to say
  *when* to call it. `:url-bound? true` shows the same fact carried as data, read by tools from `frame-meta`, and the ordering hazard vanishes because
  the engine, not the app, knows when the container is live.
-  **Regularity over cleverness** (`Principles.md:18`). Two optional artefacts hook the same frame lifecycle; one spells it as a config key and the
  other as an imperative pair. Routing already paid for the general mechanism (a post-registration hook, a preflight hook, a destroy hook); resources

**Verdict: adopt frame-owned revalidation and one explicit resolver callback contract; do not remove useful scope policies simply because the examples have not exercised them.** [The RealWorld boot sequence](../../../../examples/real-apps/realworld_resources/core.cljs) contains real ordering knowledge just to install listeners after a frame exists. [The listener implementation](../../../../implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/revalidate_listeners.cljc) already owns replacement and destruction, so putting the opt-in on the frame removes application coordination rather than merely renaming functions.

`:revalidate-on #{:focus :reconnect}` is a reasonable target. Keep this as a small resource lifecycle integration, not a general-purpose lifecycle plugin bus. Extend the existing post-registration hook path, add early configuration validation, and reconcile listeners when the frame's effective configuration changes. Preserve the existing distinction between **which host events enter a frame** and **which resources refetch for those events**; resource-level stale/owner/refetch policy still makes the latter decision. Focus means both window focus and document visibility becoming visible, not two separate public settings. JVM and non-DOM hosts remain inert.

The implementation must actually support the selected subset—the current installer always installs all three browser listeners—and handle removal, deliberate reconfiguration and destruction without stacking. Verify those behaviors against two frames, including a destroyed/recreated same-id frame, while leaving ordinary repeated `frame-root` renders free of listener churn. Do not promise that merely omitting a key during an incidental ensure call is a configuration update; use the constructor's existing reconfiguration semantics.

The resolver simplification is also sound, with one important correction: [whole-db sugar](../../../../implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/scope_registry.cljc) is selected whenever metadata lacks `:inputs`, including a three-argument form carrying only `:doc`. Derive whole-db tooling information from the declaration instead of maintaining a second authored mode. Keep this separate from broader scope-policy decisions.

**The proposed two-policy restriction is not yet justified.** [Scope resolution](../../../../implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/registry.cljc) distinguishes a concrete constant, a named db-derived value and a caller-required value. A literal tenant/sandbox scope is ordinary useful data, not a redundant resolver language. `:rf.scope/from-caller` says “there is no default”; replacing it with global-plus-overrides loses that fail-closed requirement. A named resolver reading an otherwise unnecessary db slot also adds friction and state. “Every principal lives in app-db” is not a demonstrated universal constraint: a multi-tenant inspector or reusable per-call resource can legitimately receive its subject as an argument. Retain concrete and caller-required policies. The anonymous function cases are more plausible pruning candidates, but deserve a separate decision about route-context information that db-only resolvers cannot currently express.


Similarly, [clear-scope's reference form](../../../../implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/events.cljc) means resolve against the clearing event's world; a concrete scope means act on a previously selected identity. Logout needs the latter, as the example correctly shows. That timing difference is a teaching obligation, not proof that the former has no valid use. Preserve both unless intentionally narrowing the contract. Keep the old-scope capture example prominent, remove genuinely repeated defaults from teaching, and demote planner-owned events without inventing a new public lifecycle. The high-value work is boot ownership and stable callback arguments; the policy deletions can wait.

# Resources: let the frame own listeners; declare resolver inputs once

Review date: 2026-09-05. Status: proposal only. Bead: `rf2-snkw`.

New understanding from [Fable's resource review](../fable/resources-lifecycle-and-scope.md), checked against the implementation and cited consumers. Two small reductions stand out; neither requires redesigning resource loading or cache ownership.

## Finding and known use cases

| Need | Current evidence | Unnecessary choice or ceremony |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Revalidate stale, active data when the user returns or reconnects | [RealWorld resource boot](../../../../examples/real-apps/realworld_resources/core.cljs), `mount!`: creates the frame through `frame-root`, then calls `install-revalidation-listeners!` | The application must know that installation happens after the render that creates the frame. Routing's `:url-bound?` on that same frame already avoids this two-step pattern. |
| Reinstall during hot reload and remove during teardown | [Listener implementation](../../../../implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/revalidate_listeners.cljc) | Installation replaces listeners; frame destruction already calls removal. The library owns most of this lifetime but exposes separate imperative setup/removal verbs to the application. |
| Select revalidation triggers or relinquish them | Same implementation: focus/visibility and online are distinct resource causes; removal documents rotating frame ownership | A frame policy can express the choice without exposing DOM listener management. |
| Resolve a session or viewer from declared state inputs | [RealWorld scope definitions](../../../../examples/real-apps/realworld_resources/scope.cljs), [tenant-switcher testbed](../../../../testbeds/tenant_switcher/core.cljs) | These use the explicit `:inputs` map already. |
| Resolve from the whole app-db | [Scope registry](../../../../implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/scope_registry.cljc), `canonical-spec` and `reg-resource-scope` | Omitting `:inputs` changes the callback's first argument from an inputs map to raw db. The implementation immediately wraps this sugar back into `{:inputs {:db [:db []]}}`. |
| Use the registration's scope, or explicitly inspect another scope | [Resource declarations](../../../../examples/real-apps/realworld_resources/resources.cljs) and [route plans](../../../../examples/real-apps/realworld_resources/routing.cljs) | The default can be declared once. Repeating the same resolver at use sites is not required; a genuine explicit override remains useful. |
| Clear the departing user's cache on logout | [RealWorld auth](../../../../examples/real-apps/realworld_resources/auth.cljs), logout handler | It correctly resolves concrete old scopes against the incoming db before clearing authentication state. A later request to resolve “current user” would mean something else. |

## Proposed smaller API

Make browser revalidation a frame property, analogous to URL ownership:

```clojure
;; PROPOSED frame option, not supported today.
[rf/frame-root {:id :app
                :url-bound? true
                :revalidate-on #{:focus :reconnect}}
 [root-view]]
```

Remove the application-facing install/remove pair. The frame lifecycle installs the selected host listeners after creation, reconciles deliberate frame reconfiguration, and removes them on destruction. No key means no automatic host listeners; an empty set explicitly requests none. Preserve current behavior on JVM/SSR: no browser listener work. This is not an arbitrary event-source or scheduling DSL.

The practical win is deleting a setup call and its ordering instructions from a real boot function. Use existing frame feature hooks and listener bodies; no generalized lifecycle framework is called for.

For named scope resolvers, retain one callback contract: the first argument is always the declared inputs map. Require `:inputs` and remove the whole-db sugar, including the doc-only metadata variant:

```clojure
;; Existing explicit form; proposed as the only resolver grammar.
(rf/reg-resource-scope :app/scope
  {:inputs {:db [:db []]}}
  (fn [{:keys [db]} context]
    (my-scope db context)))
```

Ordinary narrower session/viewer definitions remain unchanged. The whole-db case remains possible and honest about what it reads. Do not add an unpacking flag to recreate the old callback convention.

## Scope guidance, without a larger policy redesign

Teach registration-level scope as the default and use-site scope as an override. Remove needless repeated declarations in examples when they equal the registration. For destructive scope operations such as logout cleanup, favor a concrete scope resolved from the pre-transition db; that is already the successful RealWorld pattern.

Fable additionally proposes deleting several scope-policy forms and the deferred `clear-scope` resolver form. Those are not needed for the two reductions above. I would not bundle every policy deletion into this change: first obtain the simpler boot and callback contract, while preserving programmer control over explicit tenant/session selection.

## Why this is more elegant

A frame declares its relationship to the browser; the library owns the mechanics of maintaining that relationship. A resolver declares what it reads; its function receives that same shape every time. Both remove implicit ordering or argument-shape knowledge while leaving plain maps and functions in the programmer's hands.

This is [data before magic and regularity](../../../../spec/Principles.md) in service of productivity, not more configuration for its own sake. The success criterion is less application ceremony with the same resource behavior.

## Focused acceptance evidence

Migrate RealWorld boot and exercise first mount, repeated mount, focus/tab-return, reconnect and frame destruction; verify no duplicate listeners or SSR work. Migrate the whole-db resolver tests and retain the session, viewer and tenant examples unchanged. Explicit overrides and the current logout cleanup remain working examples, not collateral API churn.

That is a fail-closed objection, not a taste one, and it is right about one thing: `from-caller` has exactly one genuine semantic that the two-shape world cannot spell. **"The scope is a per-call fact with no app-db counterpart, and forgetting it at any site is an error at that site."** Under A, a per-call resource is modelled either as `{:from-db :x/subject}` over a slot the caller writes first — where a forgotten override at one site reads the slot, fail-closed if nil but *silently under the previous subject* if stale — or as a concrete `:scope` override on every ensure and sub, which is `from-caller`'s obligation with no runtime enforcement behind it. In-repo, the per-call case has had 14 registrations, 8 route plans and every sub in five apps to appear, and has not.

Codex's second point is specific to B6: "the anonymous function cases … deserve a separate decision about route-context information that db-only resolvers cannot currently express." A route entry already carries `:params (fn [route] …)` and `:when (fn [route ctx] …)` (`routing.cljs:96–102`, `route.cljc:487–496`), so `:scope (fn [route ctx] …)` is regular with its siblings, and a tenant-in-a-path-segment app has *no other shipped way* to derive scope from the route: `:inputs` are `[:db path]` only, and `[:runtime path]` is reserved, not shipped (`016:239–241`). Deleting B6 widens that section's un-defer trigger from "a non-route site needs a path principal" to "any site does". In-repo demand is zero, and 016 itself already rules "no anonymous route-context functions as a second public scope-resolution currency" for any *new* source — B6 is grandfathered, not chosen.

**What changes now.** Nothing. rf2-kuky.35 stays dependency-blocked by rf2-kuky.34 (open, P2, unassigned at tip). rf2-kuky.33 — the other half of "the simpler boot/callback contract" — has **already landed** (closed 2026-09-06, PR #9311 rebased at e43bec83ac; `:revalidate-on` live at `spec/API.md:473`).

Ruling now does not bundle: the beads still serialise behind .34.

**What it buys.** Nothing A-with-sequencing does not, except a second look at the same census.

### D. Keep as designed

**What changes.** Nothing. Five shapes, two clear-scope forms.

**What it costs.** The recurring tax: every `reg-resource` in every new app and every AI-generated one chooses from a menu of five where two are ever used; a spec subsection, a 009 row and a warning op per shape nobody uses; a skill snippet that leads to the mismatch footgun; a `clear-scope` form whose only reachable outcome from its one motivating site is a warning. Nobody argued D on its merits — codex's position was "not yet", which is C.

## Recommendation

**A**, filed as three beads and landed (ii) → (i) now, (iii) after rf2-kuky.34 merges. The posture settles it: a redundant spelling is deleted, not deprecated, and the corpus has answered the question — 14 of 14 registrations, 8 route plans and every sub in five apps had the chance to use B3–B6 and D2 and none did. On `spec/Principles.md`: *Regularity over cleverness* (`:18–22`, "when a feature admits two shapes for the same job, designate one as canonical") — here it admits five for a job that has two; *Named things over anonymous things* (`:24–28`) — `{:from-db :realworld/viewer}` is a name a tool can list and explain, `(fn [route ctx] …)` and `(fn [] …)` are places, and `:rf.scope/from-caller` is the anti-name, "someone else will say"; *Data before magic* (`:46–50`) and *Low hidden context* (`:87–91`) — a policy is data interpreted by the runtime, and the D2 payload's meaning depends on *which* event's db happens to be current, the hidden-context hazard 016 needs a subsection to explain. The heuristic is the tell: a ~140-line dev subsystem that exists for exactly one policy is the cost of that policy made visible, and the structural fix (`{:from-db …}`, reactive re-keying) already shipped and took every consumer with it. Codex's per-call resource is real but is modelled as app state, which is where re-frame2 puts principals; the concrete `:scope` override survives for the explicit-selection case codex wants in the programmer's hands.

**Fallback if Mike disagrees:** B — keep `:rf.scope/from-caller` and its two diagnostics as the one spelling for "there is no default", and still delete B4, B5, B6 and D2. If Mike wants B6 alone held for the `[:runtime path]` question, carve it out of (iii) as its own bead with the note that its first tenant-in-path consumer ships the reserved input source.

**On each outcome.** None of the three implementation beads exists yet under rf2-kuky; the bead's description carries them fully specified as (i), (ii), (iii).
- **A:** file (ii) `api(resources): internal-ise adopt-owner / release-owner-identities` (P3), (i) `api(resources): clear-scope takes a concrete scope` (P2, with the literal-map rejection above), (iii) `api(resources): two policy shapes` (P2, `--deps blocks:rf2-kuky.34`; B6 split off if oversize); dispatch (ii) and (i) now, sequenced on `016`/`009`; close rf2-kuky.35 with the ruling.
- **B:** as A minus the B3 rows in (iii); (iii)'s spec/doc edits reword the enum to three and keep `016:119–129`.
- **C:** no filing; rf2-kuky.35 stays blocked on rf2-kuky.34 and returns with .34's PR.

## What is already settled (no decision needed)

- **rf2-kuky.33** (`:revalidate-on` frame key) is closed and on main; **rf2-kuky.34** (one `reg-resource-scope` arity, `:inputs` required) is open and dispatchable regardless of this ruling — both were two-reviewer findings.

## Codex Recommendation

Reviewed at **2026-09-06 06:49:09 UTC**, tool-observed, against HEAD **`436e2b062afed4041d688d11617005a31b4f7157`**. I read the complete dossier and rf2-kuky.35's description (14,349 characters), notes (40,348), acceptance criteria and status. It remains an **open decision**; this recommendation does not rule it. Direct tracker checks confirm rf2-kuky.33 and rf2-h3c9 are closed, while rf2-kuky.34 remains open. The [revalidation implementation](../../implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/revalidate_listeners.cljc) already carries the frame-owned contract; the [scope registrar](../../implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/scope_registry.cljc) still implements whole-db sugar.

**Choose a modified B: retain fixed concrete scopes and `:rf.scope/from-caller`; remove registration-time functions; make `clear-scope` concrete-only; retain route scope functions until an adequate named replacement ships.** None of A–D expresses this combination. Teach three semantic contracts: a fixed value (including the explicit global claim), a named derivation, or a required caller argument. These are distinct responsibilities. Counting their EDN spellings as five competing answers obscures the useful distinction.
DOSSIER ATTACHMENT (continued, part 3 of 3):
The corpus supports teaching named derivation first: I independently found the same fourteen example/testbed registrations, six global and eight `{:from-db …}`. But a fixed tenant/sandbox value is already the simplest inspectable declaration; requiring an empty-input named resolver to return that constant adds a registration and callback without improving identity. B5 is also **tested**, contrary to the table: [the skeleton tests](../../implementation/resources/test/re_frame/resources_skeleton_cljs_test.cljs), lines 253–272, explicitly register app-keyword, tuple, map and string scopes. Remove the zero-argument function tier: pure constant computations can produce a concrete registration value, and state-dependent computations belong in named resolvers with declared inputs.

`from-caller` expresses an enforceable requirement that optional overrides cannot reproduce. The [registry's event and subscription resolvers](../../implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/registry.cljc) accept an explicit scope before considering the default; without one, a caller-required registration errors. Replacing that with a db default changes the missing-argument behavior even when that default is valid. The [tenant-switcher](../../testbeds/tenant_switcher/core.cljs), particularly `cache-witness`, already shows why a selected tenant and the active tenant differ: two explicit-scope subscriptions inspect both caches simultaneously. This does not prove an existing caller-required registration consumer, but it disproves treating every use-site subject as one active principal. Putting tenant identity in required params is another valid design, expressly allowed by [Spec 016](../../spec/016-Resources.md); it does not preserve the same tenant-wide `clear-scope` grouping. Preserve the inexpensive omission check and teach it for reusable resources with no sensible default.

The heuristic is a separate choice. [The subscription implementation](../../implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/subs.cljc) compares resource id and scope, ignores params, and guesses from another scope having an owner. Legitimate parallel reads can fit that pattern. Moreover, global or named policies can still mismatch through explicit overrides, so deleting `from-caller` does **not** structurally eliminate the problem. I favor retiring this speculative warning while retaining the deterministic missing-scope errors. The cost is losing a useful development hint; existing scoped identities and ownership evidence remain available for inspection. Do not replace it with a broader guessing subsystem.

Keep B6 for now because the [route planner](../../implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/route.cljc) supplies information the named resolver cannot receive: `[:runtime …]` is explicitly rejected as reserved and named-resolver `ctx` is nil. There is another implementation correction: `resolve-entry-scope` currently handles references/functions and returns nil for **every other value**. A concrete route override does not already “stay”; adding one requires actual support. Preserve route derivation until its replacement can serve both route planning and passive reads without mirrored application state, and make any unsupported explicit route scope fail loudly instead of disappearing into inheritance.

I agree with concrete-only clearing as an intentional simplification, not because references never work. [The existing tests](../../implementation/resources/test/re_frame/resources_from_db_scope_cljs_test.cljc) cover both successful current-scope clearing and, at lines 311–333, a clear **after logout** that warns and leaves the old entry untouched. The dossier's claim that both tests still hold the user is incorrect. The strongest keep-D argument is uniform resolution at every event boundary. Nevertheless, for teardown I prefer selecting the target before enqueueing: [RealWorld logout](../../examples/real-apps/realworld_resources/auth.cljs) already does this. Reject `:from-db`-keyed maps explicitly; passing one through literal canonicalization would silently target a different identity. Keep reference resolution for the other operations and preserve the pure helper's trace-free behavior.

Implementation sequence and focused acceptance:

1. Apply the already-agreed planner-event internalization, then concrete-only clearing; serialize shared spec edits. Prove logout/account switch clears the departing scope, leaves the replacement/global scopes intact, and suppresses late replies. Reject reference payloads before changing cache state.
2. After rf2-kuky.34, remove registration functions and retire the speculative warning. Preserve fixed-value registration, caller-required event/sub failures, named-resolution failure and reactive re-keying. Exercise simultaneous tenants with identical params; retain the [scope conformance fixture](../../spec/conformance/fixtures/resources-scope-fail-closed.edn).
3. Teach named scope inheritance in the [resource pattern](../../skills/re-frame2/patterns/resources.md), including its current-user snippet. Make [Xray's policy description](../../tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/panels/resources_helpers.cljc) identify a named resolver explicitly—it currently labels reference maps merely “resolver (data)”—and reconcile its [panel specification](../../tools/xray/spec/024-Resources-Panel.md). Handle route concrete-value validation explicitly; test that supplied values are honored or rejected, never silently ignored. Add no compatibility aliases.

Verification limits: source, tests, specs, example/testbed consumers and tooling were inspected; no runtime tests, builds or browser scenarios were executed. Corpus absence is not evidence about external applications. title: api(registry): write the registrar fx-form rule into Conventions (frame-scoped, positional args verbatim)
description:
_Filed 2026-09-05 12:37:46 AUSEST by the API-review wave-3 coordinator from registration-and-testing.md (ref spellings.2); parent epic rf2-kuky. Local-only dossiers: ai/findings/API-review/{fable,codex}/ (gitignored; may be deleted)._

## Problem

Two registrars have fx forms, and they disagree on shape:

| fx | where | args |
|---|---|---|
| `:rf.fx/reg-flow` / `:rf.fx/clear-flow` | `implementation/core/src/re_frame/fx.cljc:992` / `:1003` | the registrar's positional triple `[flow-id metadata derive-fn]` / the id, verbatim |
| `:rf.fx/reg-http-interceptor` / `:rf.fx/clear-http-interceptor` | `implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/managed.cljc:226-244` / `:247-260` | a re-spelled MAP `{:id :before :after :frame}` / `{:id :frame}` |

No written rule says WHICH registrars get an fx form or what SHAPE its args take. `spec/013-Flows.md:425-447` gives the flows mechanism (a handler cannot call a registrar because that is an effect; the fx threads the dispatching frame in as `:frame`, :447). `spec/014-HTTPRequests.md` §Middleware (:827 ff.) has no fx rationale at all. `spec/Conventions.md:478-482` places the flows pair under `:rf.fx/*` as a "single principled exception" — a NAMING rule, not an existence rule. The only stated reason for the http pair is a source comment (`managed.cljc:222-225`: "a clean alternative to the fn-call shape for codebases that prefer to drive bootstrap through the dispatch surface"). The data form and the fn form of one registration disagree on shape, and nothing says they must not.

## Evidence

- Flows fx, handler-time consumers: `examples/core/flows/core.cljs:162` (`[:rf.fx/reg-flow …]` feature gate) and `:178` (`[:rf.fx/clear-flow :cart/discount-rate]`); `examples/real-apps/realworld_http/article_editor.cljs:302`. A designed dual with a mechanism discriminator (013:447).
- Http fx: `git grep -n -E ':rf\.fx/(reg|clear)-http-interceptor' -- examples testbeds tools ':!**/test/**'` → nothing. Both shipped http examples register at boot with the macro (`examples/real-apps/realworld_http/core.cljs:445`, `realworld_resources/core.cljs:358`). Consumers are `implementation/http/test/re_frame/http_interceptors_test.clj:880-1030` and the conformance corpus (`spec/conformance/fixtures/http-interceptor-before-transforms.edn`, `http-interceptor-clear.edn`, `implementation/core/src/re_frame/conformance.cljc:267-380`, `spec/conformance/README.md:539-540`).

## Target

One paragraph in `spec/Conventions.md`, in the reserved-fx-ids section beside the `:rf.fx/*` carve-out (:478-482), with its own heading so 013 and 014 can anchor to it:

> **When a registrar has an fx form.** An fx form exists for a registrar only when the registrar is frame-scoped — the effect threads the dispatching frame in as `:frame` — and a handler-time registration has a named consumer. Its args are the registrar's positional argument vector, verbatim: the effect is `(apply reg-x args)` with the frame threaded, and the fx form never re-spells the registrar's arguments. Members: `:rf.fx/reg-flow` / `:rf.fx/clear-flow` (013 §Dynamic toggle via fx).

Plus, until @spellings.3 Q3 is ruled, ONE sentence: "`:rf.fx/reg-http-interceptor` / `:rf.fx/clear-http-interceptor` carry map args and have no shipped handler-time consumer; their disposition is open under <@spellings.3's id>." The ruling's implementation bead deletes or rewrites that sentence.

Cross-pointers (not hot-zone): `spec/013-Flows.md:425-447` cites the rule; `spec/014-HTTPRequests.md` §Middleware gains one sentence beside its fx mention pointing at the rule; `managed.cljc:222-225` comment cites the rule instead of restating its own rationale.

Do NOT delete, reshape or re-document the http pair here — @spellings.3 Q3.

## Corroboration

One-reviewer. Codex agrees a written rule is the missing piece and corrects one clause: "HTTP interceptors ARE frame-scoped and their effects deliberately carry the dispatching frame. They satisfy that half of the proposed rule; what is absent is a shipped handler-time consumer." The paragraph above is written so both statements are true at tip.

## Deletion list

None.

## Consumers to migrate

None.

## Spec, docs, examples, skills, tests

- `spec/Conventions.md` (HOT-ZONE): the paragraph. `spec/013-Flows.md`, `spec/014-HTTPRequests.md`: one pointer each. `spec/API.md`: untouched.
- `implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/managed.cljc:222-225`: comment.
- No manifest change (no var moves). No skills change (`skills/re-frame2/references/cross-cutting/api-cheatsheet.md:86` documents the http fx as it is; leave for Q3).
- Gates: `mkdocs build --strict` (spec/ staged by the hook) and `python scripts/check_doc_slugs.py` for the new anchor; the paragraph is prose, so verify the anchor and the 013/014 links by hand and say so in the PR body.

## Sequencing and hot-zone

Conventions.md is HOT-ZONE — serialise AFTER @spellings.1 (which rewrites the adjacent Convention-A / `*` tables). Not blocked by @spellings.3: the rule is tip-true; the ruling edits one sentence.

## Risks

Prose only. The one way to get it wrong is to write the consumer clause as if the http pair already failed it — that is the ruling's to say.

title: Test-suite pruning, fifth pass: implementation/machines
description:
Child of rf2-nvxtm (test-suite pruning, fifth pass). One worktree, one PR.

SURFACE: implementation/machines. This is the surface of rf2-txsk5.14 (fourth pass). Read rf2-txsk5.14 first: its description, notes and close reason. Together they give the runners and lanes, the count floors, the surface's cautions, the covers it relied on, and what the fourth pass already pruned. In the fourth pass this surface was split. rf2-txsk5.14 covered only part of it, and rf2-txsk5.39, rf2-txsk5.40, rf2-txsk5.41, rf2-txsk5.42 took the rest. Your scope is exactly the files rf2-txsk5.14 covered (its notes and close reason list them). The rest belongs to sibling children of this epic. Confirm the scope and the runners yourself at tip in step 1, and report the delta.

<DIR> in the prompt below means this surface.

REPO MECHANICS: read rf2-nvxtm's description. Its count-floor, CLJS-lane, test-name, cross-surface-cover, hot-zone, plant and one-PR rules apply in full, and they win over anything in the prompt that seems to conflict.

== THE PROMPT (verbatim from Mike's local prompt file, which is not checked in; also in rf2-nvxtm's description)

Simplify the unit tests under implementation/machines. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside implementation/machines. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
implementation/machines to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in implementation/machines; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If implementation/machines plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside implementation/machines that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

title: The documented replacement of the route-denial 403 draws :rf.warning/multiple-status-set on every denied request; delete the SSR multi-write warnings
description:
The documented way to replace the default 403 draws `:rf.warning/multiple-status-set` on every denied request. Delete the SSR multi-write warnings.

## Why the documented path warns

Spec 011 §Route entry denial tells apps to replace the runtime's 403 with an explicit `:rf.server/set-status`, for example a 404 to hide the route. The runtime's 403 is itself an ordinary fx write: `implementation/routing/src/re_frame/routing/decisions.cljc` (~L383) does `(server-frame? frame) (conj [:rf.server/set-status 403])`.

`set-status-fx` in `implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/response.cljc` records every write under `:rf.server/_status-writes` and warns when `(> (count writes) 1)`. So the documented path warns every time, although last-write-wins is already the contract. Redirects have the same shape (`:rf.warning/multiple-redirects`).

## Change

Delete:
- `:rf.warning/multiple-status-set` and `:rf.warning/multiple-redirects`;
- `warn-on-multiple-writes!`;
- the `status-writes-key` / `redirect-writes-key` bookkeeping, including its dissoc in `error_listener.cljc` (~L475-482, ~L523).

Rewrite as plain last-write-wins:
- 011 §Multiple-status policy and the redirect line (~L889);
- the docstrings in `ssr.cljc` (~L228, ~L269);
- `docs/api/re-frame.ssr.md` (~L508);
- `docs/ssr/response.md` (~L52, ~L168).

Preserve:
- last-write-wins;
- redirect precedence;
- highest-status error settlement.

Add no exemption for framework writes. `ssr_reserved_fx_guards_test.clj` (~L179-183) reads `_status-writes` to prove a 200 was written, so it needs a different witness. `ssr_end_to_end_test.clj` (~L226-252) asserts the warnings.

## Files

- `spec/011-SSR.md` is the one `i/crlf` file in the repo. Edit it with the Edit/Write tools and check its line endings.
- **spec/009-Instrumentation.md (HOT)**, rows ~L2065-2066. The keyword-catalogue drift check needs the code and the rows removed in the same PR.

title: Unit-test pruning: machines
description:
Apply the exact requested pruning prompt recursively to implementation/machines/test. This is a distinct worker cluster under rf2-0wcq5. Production code remains unchanged except temporary hash-verified fault plants. Push a draft test-only PR, babysit all latest-head checks to green, then mark ready. A measured no-op or unexecuted-file report is valid; do not manufacture changes.

Simplify the unit tests under implementation/machines/test. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside implementation/machines/test. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
implementation/machines/test to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in implementation/machines/test; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If implementation/machines/test plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.

title: Mutation settles arm resource GC without opening a GC window, so a queued check can still collect early
description:
PR #11310 (rf2-mxjjn) gives each resource entry a GC window number, `:gc-window`, in runtime-db. `open-gc-window` bumps it at every read-path event that arms a GC timer. `gc-fired` carries the window it was armed for, and a check from an older window is `:superseded`.

One arming path opens no window: `implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/mutation_events.cljc` arms GC for keys a mutation populates or patches. An ownerless entry's GC check that is queued behind such a mutation settle can still collect the entry early, because the check's window still equals the entry's.

Fix: make that path open a window the same way, through `open-gc-window` or its equivalent, only where a timer really arms. Add one queued-delivery regression with held router drains, as in resources_gc_queued_check_cljs_test.cljc, red on trunk and green with the fix.

Optionally, add `:gc-window` to Spec 016 §Status semantics' entry-field list if that list is meant to be complete.

Found by the rf2-mxjjn worker, outside its fence. Fenced on rf2-mxjjn (PR #11310) merging. Gates: the resources JVM lane, clj-kondo, and CI's test:cljs.
notes:
== WORKER SUMMARY (PR #11317) — fixed
Fix: a mutation's success settle now opens a GC window on each entry whose GC timer it arms. That covers the populate, patch and seeded-orphan policies. It goes through the read path's own open-gc-window, which is now public in events.cljc with no other change there, called from a small open-gc-windows helper in mutation_events.cljc. A window opens only where a timer really arms: the delay is positive, the frame is a client frame, and the entry still exists, so a key the same reply removed never comes back as a phantom entry.
RED on tip 5c5f9bce5d: the new test a-check-queued-behind-a-mutation-populate-waits-for-its-window in implementation/resources/test/re_frame/resources_gc_queued_check_cljs_test.cljc uses held router drains. An ownerless settle at t=0, the mutation success reply queued at t=900, and the settle timer firing at t=1000 give the FIFO [mutation succeeded, gc-fired]. Exit 1 with 3 failures: the entry was collected at t=1000 right after the populate, its data was gone, and it was not cached at t=1999.
GREEN with the fix: the namespace ran 6 tests / 23 assertions, exit 0. The full resources JVM lane exited 0 with 543 / 1554, which matches the predicted +2 tests / +9 assertions over the 541 / 1545 baseline. clj-kondo found 0 errors.
Spec 016 Status semantics was not edited: its entry-field list is not exhaustive (:refetch-sweep is absent from it), so :gc-window was not added there.
The :cljs branch relies on CI test:cljs; every change sits outside reader conditionals.

title: Unit-test pruning: testbed-support
description:
Apply the exact requested pruning prompt recursively to tools/testbed-support/test. This is a distinct worker cluster under rf2-0wcq5. Production code remains unchanged except temporary hash-verified fault plants. Push a draft test-only PR, babysit all latest-head checks to green, then mark ready. A measured no-op or unexecuted-file report is valid; do not manufacture changes.

Simplify the unit tests under tools/testbed-support/test. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside tools/testbed-support/test. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
tools/testbed-support/test to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in tools/testbed-support/test; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If tools/testbed-support/test plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside tools/testbed-support/test that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

title: Redact :exception-message and :reason with :exception-data in the machine and flow exception projectors
description:
When the machine or flow exception projector already redacts `:exception-data` as sensitive, redact the companion exception text under the same condition: `:exception-message` and, on machines, `:reason`.

## Ruling

**Decision.** Two off-box projectors in `implementation/core/src/re_frame/classification.cljc` currently redact only `:exception-data`, the author's `ex-data` map:
- `project-machine-error-tags`, for `:rf.error/machine-action-exception`;
- `project-flow-failed-tags`, for `:rf.flow/failed`.

They do so when the machine or frame declares ANY `:sensitive` classification, or the frame is unresolvable (fail closed). The free-text `:exception-message`, and the machine's `:reason`, ride beside it unredacted. Under that same condition, and no wider, those text slots are redacted too. Ordinary errors from a machine or flow with no sensitive classification keep their message, so category-only errors stay useful.

This is the second of four beads from one ruling. It must land before the pair-MCP flip. Today a row redacted this way is stamped `:sensitive? true`, and the pair MCP drops its whole epoch, so the raw message never reaches the AI. Once the flip ships flagged epochs as projected records, that message would.

Decided 2026-10-16: Mike directed that every dossier recommendation an independent Codex review agreed with be actioned. Mike's instruction, verbatim:

> review all decisions. They now have a "Codex Recomendation" section.  Where the original
> recomendation matches the Code Recomendation, create a bead to action the decision.  And then
> remove the file.  Leave behind cases where the two differ materially.

**Decisive facts (read in source at trunk 89517e8f54):**

1. `classification.cljc:1318-1323` (`redact-exception-data-slot`) replaces only `:exception-data` with `:rf/redacted` and stamps `:sensitive? true`. It is called from:
   - `project-machine-error-tags` (`:1325-1348`), when the machine's author or frame classification has any `:sensitive`, or the frame is nil;
   - `project-flow-failed-tags` (`:1350-1366`), when the frame has any sensitive declaration, or the frame is nil.
2. The dev trace for a machine action exception carries `:exception-message ex-msg` and `:reason reason` beside `:exception-data` (`implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/lifecycle_fx/registration.cljc:155-170`). `:rf.flow/failed` carries `:exception-message` (`implementation/flows/src/re_frame/flows.cljc:328-337`). Neither text slot is touched by the projector.
3. Exception text routinely embeds the value that failed. `spec/Security.md:123-131` already tells authors to name the failure category rather than interpolate secrets. This bead closes the framework's own gap on the two projectors that already judged the record sensitive.

**Rejected options:**
- **Redact exception text on every error.** That loses useful category-only messages from code with no sensitive classification. The condition stays exactly the one that already redacts `:exception-data`.
- **Leave it, because `dispatch` already ships `:errors[*].message` raw.** That inconsistency is real, but it is not a reason to widen the leak once the pair MCP stops dropping flagged epochs.

**Supersedes:** nothing.

## Work

- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/classification.cljc`: extend the shared redaction tail (`redact-exception-data-slot`, `:1318-1323`), or its two callers, so that under the existing condition:
  - `:exception-message` becomes `:rf/redacted` when present;
  - on the machine row, `:reason` becomes `:rf/redacted` when present.
- Confirm that the `:exception` object slot on the machine trace cannot carry the message off-box. If it can, redact it under the same condition.
- Tests: extend the existing machine and flow exception-projection tests, wherever `project-machine-error-tags` / `project-flow-failed-tags` are pinned; find them with `git grep -l "machine-action-exception\|rf.flow/failed" -- 'implementation/*/test/*'`.
  - For a sensitive-classified machine and flow, the message and reason are absent and their slots read `:rf/redacted`.
  - For an unclassified machine and flow, the message survives.
- Spec: if 009's or 015's description of these projectors lists only `:exception-data`, add the two text slots. That edit must follow any other open Spec 009 bead, because 009 is a hot zone; it is optional when the spec does not enumerate the slots.

**Deliberately stays:**
- The condition itself.
- The `:sensitive? true` stamp.
- `:exception-data` redaction.
- `dispatch`'s cascade summary (`skills/re-frame2-pair/preload/re_frame2_pair/pure.cljc:360-373`). That is a separate consumer, and not this ruling.

## Sequencing

- **Hot zones touched:** none in code. `spec/009-Instrumentation.md` is touched only if its projector text enumerates the slots, so check before claiming the lane.
- **Depends on:** nothing.
- **Within this ruling:** it BLOCKS the bead "Flip re-frame2-pair-mcp's epoch tools from whole-record drop to the projected record".
- **Cross-dossier:** none known.
- `spec/011-SSR.md` is not touched.

## Evidence

- **Read in source:** all `path:line` above, at trunk 89517e8f54 (HEAD 3aaacf1cde when filed).
- **Not run:** whether the `:exception` object slot serialises its message onto the wire. Check it with a test.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Run a machine action that throws `(ex-info (str "rejected " secret) {:k secret})` in a machine with a `:sensitive` classification. Its projected `:rf.error/machine-action-exception` row has `:rf/redacted` in each of these slots:
   - `:exception-data`;
   - `:exception-message`;
   - `:reason`.
   The distinctive secret string appears nowhere in the projected row, the `:exception` slot included.
2. A flow that throws the same way, in a frame with a sensitive declaration, gives an `:rf.flow/failed` row whose `:exception-message` and `:exception-data` are both `:rf/redacted`.
3. A control case keeps its text: the same throws from a machine and a flow with no sensitive classification, in a frame that resolves, keep `:exception-message` (and the machine's `:reason`) verbatim.
4. A nil-frame case fails closed, redacting the text slots as well as `:exception-data`.
5. The relevant gates are green, with their exit codes quoted in the PR body:
   - `npm run test:cljs`;
   - `scripts/test-jvm-implementation.sh`.
notes:
== WORKER SUMMARY (PR #11368, branch worker/exception-text-redact, commit 8450ded6ff on tip a7e0979946)

Change: classification.cljc's shared tail `redact-exception-data-slot` is renamed `redact-exception-slots`. Under the UNCHANGED condition (a :sensitive machine or frame, or a nil frame), it now redacts each PRESENT text slot as well as :exception-data: :exception-message, :reason and the raw :exception. The :sensitive? stamp is unchanged. The registration.cljc docstring names the slots, and flows.cljc needed no change.

:exception slot question (the bead asked for a test): YES, it carries the message off-box. On tip, a real :sensitive machine whose action throws (ex-info (str "rejected " secret) {:k secret}) projected :exception-data :rf/redacted. But :exception was still the live ExceptionInfo, whose pr-str (the pair wire form) is #error {:cause "rejected <secret>" :data {:k <secret>} ...}. CLJS prints #error {:message ... :data ...}. So :exception is redacted under the same condition. The plain-machine control test pins the printed message.

Red on tip / green with the change (JVM, one namespace each):
- machine-data-schema-redaction-test: exit 1 (1 fail), then exit 0 (12 tests / 20 assertions).
- flows-trace-test: exit 1 (3 fails), then exit 0 (13 / 21).
- security error-slot-egress-security-cljs-test: exit 1 (3 fails), then exit 0 (3 / 7).
- scripts/test-jvm-implementation.sh: exit 0 (PASS, all artefacts).
- npm run test:cljs: relies on PR CI, test.yml job `cljs`, because the shadow-cljs lane is held.

Left for follow-up, outside the fence. Spec sentences that enumerate only :exception-data:
- spec/009 :rf.flow/failed row ("project-trace-event redacts :exception-data to :rf/redacted ... the flows analogue of project-machine-error-tags");
- spec/005 machine-owned classification ("A thrown action's :exception-data is whole-slot scrubbed ...");
- spec/013 failure item 2 ("The :exception-data slot is redacted fail-closed ...").
Spec 015 does not enumerate the slots.

Findings not acted on, because the condition deliberately stays:
- The :on-done-callback and destroy-:exit machine-action-exception rows (lifecycle_fx/resolver.cljc, traces.cljc) carry :exception (and :on-done also :exception-message) but no :exception-data key, so the projector never fires on them.
- :rf.machine/guard-evaluated :outcome :threw carries a raw :exception.
- The flow condition requires non-nil :exception-data, so a plain-error flow throw keeps its message on a sensitive frame.
- The machine action row's :reason is a fixed framework sentence ("Machine action threw."); it is redacted anyway, per the ruling.

title: Exception text still leaves a sensitive machine or flow on rows that carry no :exception-data
description:
rf2-5kw8f (PR #11368) redacts `:exception-message`, `:reason` and the raw `:exception` beside `:exception-data` in the machine and flow exception projectors in `implementation/core/src/re_frame/classification.cljc`, under the ruled condition: the machine's author or frame classification declares any `:sensitive`, or the frame is unresolvable (fail closed). Its worker measured that the raw `:exception` slot DOES carry the message off-box: `pr-str` of an ExceptionInfo is `#error {:cause "<message>" :data {...} ...}` on the JVM, and CLJS prints `#error {:message ... :data ...}`.

The gap: the implementation reaches only rows that carry an `:exception-data` key, which is narrower than the ruling's condition. Under a sensitive classification these rows still ship exception text:
- the `:on-done`-callback and destroy-`:exit` `:rf.error/machine-action-exception` rows (`implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/lifecycle_fx/resolver.cljc`, `traces.cljc`) carry `:exception`, and the `:on-done` row also carries `:exception-message`, but no `:exception-data`;
- `:rf.machine/guard-evaluated` with `:outcome :threw` carries a raw `:exception`;
- `:rf.flow/failed` redacts only when `:exception-data` is non-nil, so a flow that throws a plain (non-ex-info) error keeps its message on a sensitive frame.

This is the rf2-5kw8f ruling's own condition applied to every row that carries exception text, not a widening of it: errors from code with no sensitive classification keep their message, exactly as ruled. It must land before the pair-MCP epoch flip (rf2-42gpe), for the same reason rf2-5kw8f had to: once flagged epochs ship as projected records, these slots would reach the AI.

Change: under the same condition, redact `:exception-message`, `:exception` and (machines) `:reason` on every machine- or flow-owned error/diagnostic row that carries any of them, whether or not `:exception-data` is present, and stamp `:sensitive? true` as the existing tail does. Find the rows by census of the emit sites for those slot names, not from this list.

Acceptance: for each row above, a test on a `:sensitive` machine or frame whose code throws a secret-bearing exception finds no secret in the projected row's printed form; a control on a plain machine or flow keeps the message; rf2-5kw8f's tests stay green.

Hot zones: none expected. If Spec 009's row text for these ops enumerates redacted slots, list the sentence in the PR body for a follow-up rather than editing a held 009.

description:
